title: Monte Carlo Portfolio Stress Test
text:
Overview

  
    PROBLEM
    How large can daily portfolio losses become?
    
      This project evaluates downside risk for a diversified portfolio and compares
      losses observed historically with losses generated by a Monte Carlo model.
    
  

  
    OBJECTIVE
    Compare realized and simulated tail risk
    
      Historical VaR and CVaR provide empirical downside benchmarks, while Monte
      Carlo simulation provides a simple parametric stress-testing baseline.
    
  



  
    PORTFOLIO ALLOCATION
    100%
  

  
    SPYEquities
    
    50%
  

  
    IEFBonds
    
    30%
  

  
    GLDGold
    
    20%
  

The sample contains daily adjusted market prices from 2015 through the end of 2025. The portfolio combines equities, bonds and gold to create a simple multi-asset allocation suitable for illustrating portfolio-level downside risk.

title: Monte Carlo Portfolio Stress Test
text:
Methodology

  
    01
    Market Data
    Collect adjusted daily prices for SPY, IEF and GLD.
  

  
    02
    Portfolio Returns
    Convert prices to log returns and aggregate them using fixed portfolio weights.
  

  
    03
    Historical Risk
    Estimate 99% Value at Risk and Conditional Value at Risk from realized returns.
  

  
    04
    Monte Carlo
    Generate 10,000 daily return scenarios from the historical mean and volatility.
  

Daily log returns are calculated as
\[
r_t = \ln\left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}}\right).
\]
Historical VaR identifies the loss threshold exceeded by roughly the worst 1% of observations. CVaR measures the average loss beyond that threshold.

title: Monte Carlo Portfolio Stress Test
text:
Key Results

  
    HISTORICAL VaR
    1.65%
    99% confidence
  

  
    HISTORICAL CVaR
    2.52%
    99% expected shortfall
  

  
    MONTE CARLO VaR
    1.37%
    10,000 simulations
  

  
    MONTE CARLO CVaR
    1.60%
    99% expected shortfall
  



  MAIN TAKEAWAY
  
    Historical tail losses are larger than those produced by the normal Monte
    Carlo baseline. The gap is most visible in CVaR:
    2.52% historically versus 1.60% in simulation.
  

The portfolio produced an annualized historical return of approximately 9.01% with annualized volatility of 9.64%. The largest daily loss in the sample was approximately 5.83%.

title: Monte Carlo Portfolio Stress Test
text:
Analysis

Relative asset performance
Normalizing each asset series to 100 provides a common starting point and makes the different long-run paths of equities, bonds and gold easier to compare. In practical terms, SPY is the growth engine, IEF acts as the stabilizer, and GLD provides diversification against equity stress.

  ↗
  
    Interpretation
    Comparing normalized price paths highlights how each sleeve contributes differently to return generation and diversification.
  



Historical versus simulated downside risk
The simulated normal baseline produces smaller 99% tail-risk estimates than the historical return distribution. This indicates that the simple parametric simulation understates the severity of downside outcomes observed in the sample.

  !
  
    Interpretation
    Historical downside risk remains the more conservative benchmark for this portfolio under severe conditions.
  



Monte Carlo return distribution
The simulated distribution is useful as a baseline, but it produces a thinner left tail than the historical data. This is why the Monte Carlo VaR and CVaR figures remain below the empirical historical estimates.

  ∿
  
    Interpretation
    The gap between simulated and historical tail losses suggests non-normal features such as fat tails in realized returns.
  



Historical stress episodes
Historical portfolio returns reveal periods of unusually large gains and losses. Large negative observations tend to cluster around market stress regimes rather than appearing as isolated random events.

  —
  
    Interpretation
    Stress episodes are not evenly distributed over time, which supports extending the model with time-varying volatility in future work.

title: Monte Carlo Portfolio Stress Test
text:
Conclusion
The project demonstrates a transparent workflow for moving from market prices to portfolio returns, historical tail-risk estimation and Monte Carlo stress testing.
The key comparison is between realized historical losses and a normal-distribution simulation baseline. Historical VaR and especially historical CVaR are larger, indicating that the simple parametric model does not fully reproduce the severity of downside observations present in the historical sample.
A natural next step would be to extend the framework with fat-tailed distributions, time-varying volatility, dynamic correlations, multi-day risk horizons and explicit historical crisis scenarios.

title: Monte Carlo Portfolio Stress Test
text: This project applies a Monte Carlo simulation to evaluate downside risk in a multi-asset portfolio. Historical market prices are used to construct portfolio returns, estimate historical VaR and CVaR, and generate simulated stress scenarios for potential extreme losses.

title: Monte Carlo Portfolio Stress Test
text:
1. Import libraries
The notebook uses yfinance for market data, pandas and numpy for calculations, and matplotlib for visualization.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import yfinance as yf

pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda x: f"{x:,.6f}")

title: Monte Carlo Portfolio Stress Test
text:
2. Define portfolio and analysis settings
The weights sum to 100%. The dates can be changed if a different historical sample is preferred.

tickers = ["SPY", "IEF", "GLD"]

weights = pd.Series(
    [0.50, 0.30, 0.20],
    index=tickers,
    name="Weight"
)

start_date = "2015-01-01"
end_date = "2025-12-31"

confidence_level = 0.99
simulations = 10_000
random_seed = 42

print("Portfolio weights:")
print(weights)
print("\nSum of weights:", weights.sum())

title: Monte Carlo Portfolio Stress Test
text:
7. Historical VaR and CVaR at 99%

VaR (99%) estimates the loss threshold exceeded in approximately the worst 1% of historical observations.
CVaR / Expected Shortfall (99%) is the average loss conditional on being beyond that VaR threshold.

The notebook reports losses as positive percentages for easier interpretation.

tail_probability = 1 - confidence_level

historical_threshold = np.quantile(portfolio_returns, tail_probability)
historical_var_99 = -historical_threshold

historical_tail = portfolio_returns[portfolio_returns <= historical_threshold]
historical_cvar_99 = -historical_tail.mean()

print(f"Historical VaR (99%):  {historical_var_99:.2%}")
print(f"Historical CVaR (99%): {historical_cvar_99:.2%}")
print(f"Historical tail observations: {len(historical_tail)}")

Historical VaR (99%):  1.65%
Historical CVaR (99%): 2.52%
Historical tail observations: 28

title: Monte Carlo Portfolio Stress Test
text:
8. Monte Carlo simulation
A simple parametric Monte Carlo model is used. It assumes daily portfolio returns follow a normal distribution with the historical mean and standard deviation.
This is intentionally a simple baseline stress model. Real financial returns can exhibit skewness, fat tails, volatility clustering, and regime changes.

np.random.seed(random_seed)

mean_return = portfolio_returns.mean()
std_return = portfolio_returns.std()

simulated_returns = np.random.normal(
    loc=mean_return,
    scale=std_return,
    size=simulations
)

print("Number of simulations:", len(simulated_returns))
print(f"Simulated mean return: {simulated_returns.mean():.4%}")
print(f"Simulated volatility:  {simulated_returns.std(ddof=1):.4%}")

Number of simulations: 10000
Simulated mean return: 0.0345%
Simulated volatility:  0.6092%

title: Monte Carlo Portfolio Stress Test
section: 9. Monte Carlo 99% stress loss and Expected Shortfall
text:
9. Monte Carlo 99% stress loss and Expected Shortfall
The 1st percentile of simulated returns is the 99% downside threshold. Expected Shortfall averages simulated returns that fall below that threshold.

mc_threshold = np.quantile(simulated_returns, tail_probability)
mc_var_99 = -mc_threshold

mc_tail = simulated_returns[simulated_returns <= mc_threshold]
mc_cvar_99 = -mc_tail.mean()

print(f"Monte Carlo VaR / Stress Loss (99%): {mc_var_99:.2%}")
print(f"Monte Carlo CVaR (99%):             {mc_cvar_99:.2%}")
print(f"Simulated tail observations:        {len(mc_tail)}")

Monte Carlo VaR / Stress Loss (99%): 1.37%
Monte Carlo CVaR (99%):             1.60%

title: Monte Carlo Portfolio Stress Test
text:
Conclusion
This notebook evaluates downside risk for a diversified portfolio consisting of equities, bonds, and gold. Historical VaR and CVaR summarize extreme losses observed in the sample, while the Monte Carlo simulation generates additional return scenarios based on the portfolio’s historical mean and volatility.
The model provides a transparent baseline for portfolio stress testing. A more advanced version could incorporate non-normal return distributions, time-varying volatility, correlations that change during crises, multi-day horizons, and explicit historical crisis scenarios.
